turns.prompt_text: how do I find videos within the developer tools menu in Firefox on Mac?
turns.response_html:
To find and inspect videos using the Firefox Developer Tools on a Mac, you can use a few different tabs depending on whether you want to see the video file itself, its network performance, or the underlying HTML code.

Here is the most effective way to locate them:

1. The Network Tab (Best for finding the source file)

If you want to find the direct URL of a video or see if it is loading correctly, the Network tab is your best bet.

  • Open Developer Tools: Press Cmd + Option + I (or right-click anywhere and select Inspect).
  • Select "Network": Click the Network tab at the top of the inspector pane.
  • Filter by Media: In the small filter bar below the main tabs, click on Media. This will hide images, scripts, and documents, showing only audio and video files.
  • Reload the Page: You may need to refresh the page (Cmd + R) while the Network tab is open to see the video files populating the list.
  • Identify the file: Look for files with types like .mp4, .webm, or m4s (for streaming). You can right-click the file name and select Open in New Tab to view or download it directly.

2. The Inspector Tab (Best for seeing how it's embedded)

If you want to see the actual <video> tag or the container holding it:

  • Use the Picker Tool: Click the Select Element icon (the small square with a cursor) in the top-left corner of the Developer Tools window.
  • Click the Video: Click directly on the video player on the webpage.
  • View the Code: The Inspector tab will jump to the highlighted HTML. Look for:
    • <video> tags.
    • <iframe> tags (common for YouTube or Vimeo embeds).
    • <div> containers with background videos.

3. The Media Dashboard (Advanced Debugging)

Firefox has a specific hidden tool for inspecting media playback called the Media Panel.

  • While the Developer Tools are open, click the three dots (⋯) or the "double chevron" (>>) at the far right of the tab list (Inspector, Console, etc.).
  • Select Media.
  • This panel provides a detailed breakdown of every media element on the page, including its resolution, bitrate, and any decoder errors that might be happening.

turns.prompt_text: all right, so I'm not seeing it in the network tab. However, in the debugger, I see an area where I could be. I'm looking for where they make the API call.
turns.response_html:
If it’s not showing up as a simple "Media" file in the Network tab, the site is likely using HLS (HTTP Live Streaming) or DASH. Instead of one big video file, the browser downloads hundreds of tiny .ts or .m4s "segments" via API-style fetch calls.

In the Debugger tab, you can track down exactly which script is making those calls. Here is how to find the "smoking gun":

1. Look for XHR/Fetch Breakpoints

The Debugger allows you to pause the code the exact millisecond an API call is made.

  • In the Debugger tab, look at the right-hand sidebar.
  • Find the XHR Breakpoints section.
  • Click the + icon and leave it blank (to break on any call) or type a keyword like video, playlist, or m3u8.
  • Now, play the video. Firefox will "pause" the execution on the line of JavaScript that triggered the request.

2. Search Across All Source Files

If you want to find the logic responsible for the API call without pausing:

  • Press Cmd + Shift + F while in the Debugger. This opens a global search.
  • Search for common video API terms:
    • fetch(
    • XMLHttpRequest
    • .m3u8 (The manifest file for HLS)
    • .mpd (The manifest file for DASH)
    • video/mp4

3. Trace the Call Stack

Once you find a suspicious script or hit a breakpoint:

  • Look at the Call Stack (right sidebar).
  • This shows the "ladder" of functions that led to the API call. You can click through them to see which higher-level function (e.g., loadVideoPlayer) started the process.

Why it might be "hidden"

If the API call returns a Blob URL (looks like blob:https://site.com/...), the video is being assembled in the browser's memory. In that case, the Network tab won't show a .mp4 because the "file" doesn't technically exist on the server in that format.

Since you've worked with asynchronous architectures and camera frame translation before, you might find it useful to check the Console as well—often, developers leave console.log statements for API responses that reveal the endpoint structure.

Would you like me to help you interpret a specific API response or a blob URL if you find one?

That sounds like a heartbeat request. In web video players, requestHb (or similar names like sendHeartbeat, ping, or trackHb) is a common function used to send periodic status updates back to a server while you are watching a video.

Since you've worked with asynchronous systems and camera frame logic, you can think of this as a telemetry loop. It usually triggers every 10–60 seconds to report:

  • How much of the video you've watched (playback position).
  • Buffer health (to see if the video is stuttering).
  • User engagement (checking if the tab is still active).

How to use this to find the Video API

If you are seeing requestHb in the Debugger, you are likely looking at the tracking or analytics script, not the core video loader. However, it's a great "trail of breadcrumbs" to find the real API.

Here is how to pivot from that function to the actual video source:

1. Check the Call Stack While paused on requestHb:

  • Look at the Call Stack pane on the right.
  • Look for function names like initPlayer, setupMedia, or loadManifest.
  • If you see a call coming from a different file (e.g., player.js or vendor-video.js), click that file in the stack. That is usually where the actual video stream URL is requested.

2. Inspect the "requestHb" Variables If you hover over the variables inside that function (or look at the Scopes pane), look for an object often called mediaConfig, playerState, or source. It often contains the Master Playlist URL (.m3u8 or .mpd) which is what you're ultimately after.

3. Set a "Breakpoint on XHR" for the heartbeat If requestHb is making an actual network call:

  • Right-click the function name in the Debugger and select Add XHR Breakpoint.
  • The next time it fires, it will pause. Then, switch to the Network tab. The last request made before the heartbeat is often the most recent video segment or the metadata call.

A Common Pattern in "HB" Scripts

Often, the code looks something like this:

function requestHb(data) {
    fetch('/api/v1/telemetry', { 
        method: 'POST', 
        body: JSON.stringify({ 
            videoId: player.currentId, // <--- This ID is what you want!
            position: player.currentTime 
        }) 
    });
}

If you see a videoId or contentId being passed into that heartbeat, you can then search the Network tab or Debugger (Cmd + Shift + F) for that specific ID string. That will usually lead you straight to the API call that initializes the video.
